value: swimming time and spatial use of the aquarium differed significantly among the four underwater playback conditions
units: categorical (behavioural response to playback; significance among conditions)

source.authors: Giovanni de Vincenzi, Primo Micarelli, Salvatore Viola, Gaspare Buffa, Virginia Sciacca, Vincenzo Maccarrone, Valentina Corrias, Francesca Romana Reinero, Cristina Giacoma, Francesco Filiciotto
source.title: Biological Sound vs. Anthropogenic Noise: Assessment of Behavioural Changes in Scyliorhinus canicula Exposed to Boats Noise

method: behavioural playback in aquarium: swimming time and position (up/down and left/right sections) scored under four acoustic conditions; Kruskal-Wallis test on swimming time; not a threshold or audiogram
conditions: Twelve small-spotted catsharks (6 females, 6 males; 228 +/- 23 g, 39.3 +/- 0.8 cm) drawn from 22 wild animals trawled between Elba Island and Sardinia and held about a month at an aquarium before testing; each shark was used in one 10-min trial after 10 min habituation, individually in an aquarium; 12 trials in random order, three per condition. Conditions: control (aquarium background only), biological sounds (snapping shrimp, sea-urchin grazing, Sciaena umbra calls), biological 6 dB above anthropogenic (hydrofoil, ferry, fishing and recreational boats), and biological 6 dB below anthropogenic; amplitude set between 100 and 140 dB re 1 uPa; the speaker has a limited frequency response below about 200 Hz, so low-frequency content was not reproduced faithfully. Results text gives Kruskal-Wallis H = 39.4, N = 96, df = 3, p = 0.0005 for swimming time; the greatest swimming increase was in the biological-below-anthropogenic condition and no significant differences were found among the other conditions. The Abstract states the spatial result qualitatively (tendency to occupy the least noisy sections) and the sentence quoted gives no test statistic for spatial use. The study shows reaction to sound, not hearing sensitivity.
quote: The results highlighted significant differences in swimming time and in the spatial use of the aquarium among the experimental conditions.

units: % escape response probability to a simulated approaching predator (mean over all treatments)

source.authors: Zahra M. Bagheri, Callum G. Donohue, Julian C. Partridge, Jan M. Hemmi
source.title: Behavioural and neural responses of crabs show evidence for selective attention in predator avoidance

method: behavioural: escape response of crabs in the field-like arena to computer-generated dark looming disks (single or paired), scored for response probability and timing; treatment order by Latin square
conditions: Wild fiddler crabs collected from intertidal mudflats near Broome, Western Australia and housed at the University of Western Australia; behavioural experiments used 50 crabs (25 females, 25 males) (the Methods sentence also lists 23 crabs for the intracellular experiments). Stimuli were 30 mm dark disks on a collision course approaching at 200 mm/s from 5000 mm, at -100% Weber contrast in Experiment 1 and -40% and -100% in Experiment 2; stimuli single or paired (paired disks separated by 90 or 180 degrees); a stationary grey horizontal bar kept the eyes aligned; at least 3 min acclimatisation and at least 3 min between stimuli, and each crab saw at most two stimuli, on alternate days. The 75.4% is the average across all treatments, not a threshold; the paper reports that in Experiment 1 response probability and timing did not differ between treatments (one versus two predators, 90 versus 180 degree separation), and that responses to the low-contrast stimulus occurred significantly later (p = 0.004).
